articoli.rubrica: Draft cost-benefit analysis/impact assessment
articoli.testo:
5.1. Draft cost-benefit analysis/impact assessment
1. Article 16(2) of Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council
of 24 November 2010 establishing a European Supervisory Authority (European Banking
Authority) (EBA Regulation) provides that the EBA should carry out an analysis of ‘the potential
related costs and benefits’ of any guidelines it develops. This analysis should provide an
overview of the findings regarding the problem to be dealt with, the solutions proposed and
the potential impact of these options.
A. Problem identification and policy objectives
2. Directive 2013/36/EU was amended in 2021, following the entry into force of Directive (EU)
2019/878. The update of the Guidelines is needed following the entry into force of Directive
(EU) 2024/1619. Consistency with other EBA regulatory products should also be ensured.
3. The 2026 amendments to the guidelines aim at:
• specifying further the requirements introduced by Article 48g of Directive 2013/36/EU on
third-country branches’ sound internal governance arrangements, taking into account
third-country branches’ specificities and the application of proportionality.
• ensuring that institutions draw up, maintain and update individual statements setting out
the roles and duties of all members of the management body in its management function,
of senior management and of key function holders and a mapping of duties, according to
Article 88(3) of Directive 2013/36/EU.
• ensuring that the simplification and burden reduction objectives are implemented as stated
in the EBA action plan (TFE Recommendation 2.2) endorsed by the EBA Board of Supervisors
in December 2025 while preserving sound governance arrangements.
B. Baseline scenario
4. The current EU legislative framework for institutions’ internal governance consists mainly of
Directive 2013/36/EU and its subsequent amendments, the EBA guidelines on internal
governance, the EBA Guidelines on the assessment of the suitability of members of the
management body and key function holders and the EBA Guidelines on third-party risk
management (formerly Guidelines on outsourcing), and the EBA Guidelines on management
of ESG risks.

articoli.rubrica: The impact assessment covers the guidelines developed to ensure a consistent and
articoli.testo:
5. The impact assessment covers the guidelines developed to ensure a consistent and
harmonised application of additional governance requirements applicable to institutions
introduced by Directive 2013/36/EU and areas where the policy has changed. Areas that have
not changed in substance and the underlying changes introduced by Directive 2013/36/EU and
Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 have not been assessed.
C. Options considered
Changes made in 2026 58
6. Directive (EU) 2024/1619 (CRD VI) introduces amendments to Directive 2013/36/EU to ensure
that third-country branches have sound internal governance arrangements. These
requirements form part of the harmonised framework for third-country branches established
within the EU, which was introduced in light of the material footprint that some of these
branches have in the EU banking sector and the resulting risks to financial stability in the EU,
as well as the currently fragmented prudential and supervisory requirements to which they
were subject. The impact of the introduction of those requirements into the Directive has been
assessed in the legislative process and is not considered in this impact assessment.

articoli.rubrica: While the specifications regarding the requirements for third-country branches in the
articoli.testo:
7. While the specifications regarding the requirements for third-country branches in the
Guidelines are new, third-country branches were already expected to comply with internal
governance requirements and were already in the scope of the Guidelines on internal
governance published in 2021. Certain aspects of these requirements were also reflected in
the EBA Opinion on the set-up and operationalisation of Intermediate EU Parent
Undertaking(s) under Article 21b of Directive 2013/36/EU. In this context, the implementation
and compliance costs resulting from the additional clarifications provided by the Guidelines
are expected to be limited.
8. CRD VI also introduced a requirement that institutions need to draw up, maintain and update
individual statements setting out the roles and duties of all members of the management body
in its management function, senior management and key function holders. The Guidelines
provide additional details on how these individual statements should be prepared, taking into
account a proportionate approach, and include an optional template in the Annex. The options
of not providing a template and of introducing a mandatory template were both considered
but ultimately disregarded to provide institutions with as much guidance as possible while
limiting the potential constraints associated with a mandatory template. Given that the
preparation of individual statements is already a requirement under the Directive, and that
the template is optional, the costs resulting from these additional clarifications provided by
the Guidelines are expected to be limited. In addition, all the required information to complete
the necessary documentation is already available within institutions.
For the previous amendments to the Guidelines made in 2021 and earlier, please refer to the impact assessments of
those versions of the Guidelines that are available on the EBA’s website.
9. Similarly, institutions are required to draw up, maintain and update a mapping of duties,
including details of reporting lines, areas of responsibility and the persons involved in the
governance arrangements. Given that the mapping of duties depends on institutions’
organisational structures and specific characteristics, no template was considered appropriate
for this requirement. The approach is principles-based and provides institutions with the
flexibility to present the mapping of duties in the manner they consider most appropriate,
provided that the relevant guidance is complied with. Given that the mapping of duties is
already a requirement under Directive 2013/36/EU, the costs resulting from these additional
clarifications provided by the Guidelines are expected to be negligible. Furthermore, all the
relevant information is already available within institutions.
10. The Guidelines also required the redrafting of certain sections to reflect the findings of the EBA
benchmarking report on diversity practices and gender-neutral remuneration policies, the
consideration of ESG risks in the short, medium and long term within the prudential framework
in accordance with Article 87a of Directive 2013/36/EU and the EBA Guidelines on the
management of ESG risks, as well as the changes resulting from the entry into force of the
digital operational resilience framework under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554. These changes are
not expected to entail significant implementation costs, as they primarily ensure consistency
with new or existing regulatory requirements.
Simplification and burden reduction
11. The revised Guidelines are expected to contribute to simplification and burden reduction
objectives while preserving the underlying prudential objectives. In response to stakeholders’
feedback, several provisions have been streamlined, reformulated at a higher level and made
more principles-based. The revised text places greater emphasis on proportionality, allowing
institutions and third-country branches to implement the requirements in a manner that is
commensurate with their size, internal organisation, and the nature, scope and complexity of
their activities.
12. Administrative burden is reduced through, among other measures, the possibility of relying on
existing repositories of governance documents, including within the group, for the preparation
and maintenance of individual statements and mappings of duties, the removal of duplicative
or overly prescriptive requirements, the deletion of provisions that overlap with existing
regulatory frameworks, and the simplification of diversity and inclusion monitoring
expectations. The clarification of the scope of application for third-country branches and the
more targeted approach to conflicts of interest are expected to enhance legal certainty and
facilitate implementation.
D. Cost-benefit analysis
13. Given the limited amendments introduced by CRD VI regarding governance arrangements, the
changes to the Guidelines are expected to result in no, or only very limited, implementation
costs for third-country branches and for institutions with regard to the implementation of
individual statements and mapping of duties. Furthermore, regarding individual statements
and mapping of duties, the information required is already available within institutions, which
further limits any additional compliance and operational costs.
14. In line with the simplification and burden reduction objectives and taking into account the
application of the principle of proportionality, the Guidelines provide institutions with
sufficient flexibility in the implementation of the governance requirements and avoid imposing
unnecessary administrative burdens, including through the use of an optional template for
individual statements and a principles-based approach for the mapping of duties.
15. While a limited implementation effort may be required to review governance frameworks and
adapt internal documentation where necessary, the resulting costs are expected to be low.
This is because most of the requirements either reflect obligations already introduced by
Directive 2013/36/EU or clarify existing supervisory expectations. In addition, the relevant
information and governance arrangements are already available within institutions and third-
country branches in most cases. The revised Guidelines have been updated considering
implementation burden reduction. Compared with the consultation draft, the final text adopts
a more principles-based and proportionate approach, removes unnecessary prescriptiveness
and simplifies a number of requirements.

articoli.rubrica: Additional burden-reduction measures include the deletion of Annex I, which largely
articoli.testo:
16. Additional burden-reduction measures include the deletion of Annex I, which largely
duplicated provisions already contained in the main body of the Guidelines, the removal of the
standalone section on the general policy for third-party risk management, which is already
covered by dedicated regulatory frameworks, and the simplification of diversity and inclusion
provisions through a less prescriptive and more principles-based approach. These changes are
expected to reduce compliance costs and administrative burdens, particularly for smaller and
non-complex institutions.
17. The revised Guidelines also improve proportionality and legal certainty. For third-country
branches, the clearer distinction between applicable and non-applicable provisions and the
more targeted application of governance requirements are expected to facilitate
implementation and supervisory assessment. Similarly, the clarification of conflict-of-interest
provisions and the more targeted cooling-off framework provide greater flexibility while
maintaining appropriate safeguards. These clarifications reduce uncertainty and may lower
implementation and interpretation costs for institutions and supervisors.
18. The Guidelines improve clarity, consistency and supervisory convergence across the Union,
while preserving the key prudential objectives of sound governance, clear accountability and
effective risk management.
19. Overall, the revised Guidelines provide a more operational and proportionate framework,
reducing compliance costs and implementation efforts for institutions and competent
authorities without compromising supervisory effectiveness or governance standards.

articoli.rubrica: Views of the Banking Stakeholder Group (BSG)59
articoli.testo:
5.2. Views of the Banking Stakeholder Group (BSG)59
The Banking Stakeholder Group (BSG) stresses that the guidelines should be interpreted with broad
flexibility, taking into account not only the size, complexity, and risk profile of institutions, but also
the diversity of national governance frameworks and board structures across the European Union.
They consider that the principle of proportionality is fundamental and should allow institutions to
design their governance structures in a manner proportionate to their specific circumstances.
According to the BSG, certain sections of the guidelines are overly prescriptive and detailed and
could hinder the ability of management to respond efficiently to changing business needs.
The group suggests that the mapping of duties and individual statements requirements are
burdensome without improving governance quality. The BSG recommends a more principles-based
approach, asserting that existing documentation such as organisational charts and job descriptions
should be sufficient to meet regulatory expectations.
Regarding board roles and executive functions, the BSG advises that flexibility should be retained
for the chair of the management body to assume executive functions, provided that appropriate
checks and balances are in place. They warn against imposing a uniform governance model that
does not reflect the diversity of legal frameworks across Member States. Furthermore, the BSG
argues that stricter requirements on the compatibility of roles within groups and the introduction
of a three-year cooling-off period go beyond the requirements of CRD VI and may conflict with
national law.
The BSG also finds the requirement for both individual and collective ESG expertise for
remuneration committee members unnecessarily strict and inconsistent with other EBA guidelines,
suggesting that collective knowledge should be sufficient.
They support the monitoring of gender diversity but recommend that the list of KPIs be reviewed
to avoid overlap with other regulations, such as the CSRD and Pay Transparency Directive, and that
institutions should have the flexibility to select indicators appropriate to their context.
The group requests clarification that the compliance function should be responsible for
“compliance risk” rather than the broader “legal risk,” to avoid confusion with the responsibilities
of the legal department.
The BSG also questions the requirement for BCP documentation to be stored on “physically
separated systems,” as this is not found in DORA or other EBA guidelines and may cause ambiguity.
The full BSG response is available under: https://www.eba.europa.eu/publications-and-media/events/consultation-
revised-guidelines-internal-governance-under-crd

articoli.testo:
5.3. Feedback on the public consultation and on the opinion of
the Banking Stakeholder Group (BSG)
The EBA publicly consulted on the draft proposal contained in this paper.
The consultation period lasted for 3 months and ended on 7 November 2025. 24 responses were
received, of which 22 were published on the EBA website, the other 2 being submitted
confidentially. The BSG also submitted its opinion.
This paper presents a summary of the key points and other comments arising from the consultation,
the analysis and discussion triggered by these comments and the actions taken to address them if
deemed necessary.
In many cases several industry bodies made similar comments, or the same body repeated its
comments in the response to different questions. In such cases, the comments and EBA analysis
are included in the section of this paper where the EBA considers them most appropriate.
Changes to the draft Guidelines have been incorporated as a result of the responses received during
the public consultation.
Summary of key issues and the EBA’s response
Stakeholders broadly supported the principle of proportionality but requested clearer criteria, such
as size or complexity, to determine simplified governance requirements. Concerns were raised
about disproportionate compliance costs for small institutions.
Several respondents objected to removing references to national company law and called for
reinstating definitions for key roles like CEO and heads of control functions.
On management bodies and committees, stakeholders welcomed clarification of roles but found
mapping duties and individual statements too granular. Annex II’s mapping requirements were
criticised as overly detailed. Respondents suggested using existing documentation and limiting
mapping to management functions.
Restrictions on intra-group roles and cooling-off periods for former CEOs were strongly opposed as
exceeding CRD VI and reducing flexibility. Most called for deletion or revision of these provisions.
On ESG and risk management, stakeholders agreed on integration but warned against
disproportionate emphasis. Respondents opposed mandatory individual ESG expertise in
remuneration committees, preferring collective competence and flexibility in composition.
Stakeholders supported gender-neutral policies but requested flexibility in monitoring and
reporting.
For third-country branches, stakeholders supported harmonisation, but highlighted challenges in
applying all requirements considering that branches do not have their own legal personality. They
sought clarity on ‘sufficient presence,’ delegation, and proportionality, noting that not all group-
level rules should apply.
Internal control functions’ independence was supported, but requirements were seen as rigid.
Respondents requested flexibility in combining risk and compliance roles and objected to
terminology changes that blurred distinctions between compliance and legal functions.
Business continuity requirements were generally supported, but respondents sought clarification
on terms and consistency with DORA.
EBA’s response
The EBA Guidelines aim to specify further the governance provisions of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD)
as amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1619 (CRD VI).
The Guidelines apply in a proportionate way and remain open to different national company laws.
Definitions removed from the Guidelines are largely directly included in the Directives and apply
also in the context of these Guidelines.
While institutions are required to promote gender neutrality and diversity, the indicators included
represent examples and good practices rather than a mandatory list of indicators to be
implemented. However, to introduce a more proportionate approach, the indicators have been
removed.
Regarding the business continuity requirements, the Guidelines have been more closely aligned
with DORA and the BCBS principles, given the different context, i.e. general high-level principles
versus more detailed specific ICT related requirements that apply under DORA; some more general
language has been used.
The provisions on the mapping of duties, interplay between the compliance and legal functions, and
conflicts of interest have been reviewed and comments taken into account where appropriate while
ensuring that sound governance arrangements are preserved.
